6. 
Substantive (or '^Organic'') Agency Statutes and Procedural 
Requirements for Rulemaking. The primary focus of this chapter is on the 
APA’s role (as interpreted by the courts) in establishing the procedural 
requirements that federal agencies must follow in order to issue regulatory 
rules. As we have seen, the APA governs matters such as whether an agency 
needs to use notice-and-comment or trial-type procedures before issuing rules. 
It also furnishes a statutory basis for the requirement that agencies explain 
the legal and poHcy basis for rules when final rules are published in the Federal 
Register. See United States v. Nova Scotia Food Products Corp., infra.
But rulemaking requirements may also arise because of provisions in 
what we described in Chapter 2 as the agency’s “authorizing legislation.” This 
may include the substantive (sometimes also called “organic”) statutes that 
originally created the agency, as well as subsequent statutes that provide legal 
authority for agencies to regulate. Authorizing statutes may call for an agency 
I
to make special findings about the impact of a regulatory rule, for example, 
;
before the rule takes effect. Rather than preempting analytical requirements 
.
in substantive agency statutes, the APA’s judicial review provisions have been 
understood to help give effect to those requirements.
As State Farm illustrates, courts following the APA are supposed to strike 
down agency actions that are arbitrary or capricious. While the scope of review 
under the “arbitrary and capricious” standard is supposed to be relatively 
narrow, agency rules are nonetheless subject to invahdation as arbitrary and 
capricious when, inter alia, the agency has reUed on factors which Congress 
has not intended it to consider, or entirely failed to consider an important 
aspect of the problem. An analytical requirement found in an agency’s 
authorizing legislation constitutes one such “important aspect of the problem.” 
<•
Failure to adhere to such a requirement can be viewed as simultaneously a 
procedural and a substantive failing. 
*
Hence, courts will invahdate agency rulemaking that does not adhere to 
the analytical requirements promulgated by authorizing legislation. For 
instance, in Public Citizen v. Federal Motor Carrier Safety Admin., 374 F.3d 
J
1209, 1216 (D.C. Cir. 2004), the D.C. Circuit struck down a rule regulating 
permissible driving hours of commercial motor vehicle drivers as arbitrary and 
capricious because the agency neglected to consider a factor mandated by 
statute. The Interstate Commerce Commission Termination Act directs the 
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration to issue rules related to truck 
driver fatigue—^but only after collecting and analyzing data on certain costs 
and benefits. Because the agency wholly failed to consider the impact of its 
rules on the health of drivers as the organic statute directed, this sin gio 
objection from petitioners was sufficient to justify the court’s conclusion that
